resolved_by: Supreme Court in United States v. Castleman, 572 U.S. 157 (2014), which the opinion says resolved the conflict against the Tenth Circuit's Perez-Vargas and Rodriguez-Enriquez line
issue: Under the elements clause of 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)(3)(A), does 'physical force' require force applied directly to the victim, or does it also include indirect force, such as causing bodily injury by poison?

sides.position: 'Physical force' requires force imparted directly, so an offense that can be committed indirectly (for example, by poisoning or deception) does not qualify as a crime of violence.
cases: United States v. Rodriguez-Enriquez, 518 F.3d 1191 (10th Cir. 2008)
United States v. Muskett, 970 F.3d 1233 (10th Cir. 2020)

sides.position: 'Physical force' includes indirect force, so an assault that causes bodily injury through indirect means qualifies as a crime of violence.
cases: United States v. Juvenile Female, 566 F.3d 943 (9th Cir. 2009)

this_court: Adopts the indirect-force position. The court overruled Perez-Vargas in Ontiveros, 875 F.3d 533 (10th Cir. 2017), and states that Castleman resolved the conflict against Perez-Vargas and Rodriguez-Enriquez.
quote: Thus, the circuits were in disagreement as to whether “physical force” encompassed indirect force when Mr. Muskett committed his crime.
cite: United States v. Muskett, 970 F.3d 1233 (10th Cir. 2020)
